opus-5.5.text:
Pre-training is one of those things that's very easy to describe and very hard to fully understand. The easy description is that you take an enormous amount of text, essentially a large fraction of what people have written, and you train a neural network to predict the next word. That's it. But I think the simplicity of the objective hides how much is actually going on.

Here's the way I like to think about it. If you want to predict the next word really well, not just okay but *really* well, you have to understand a great deal about the process that generated the text. And the process that generated the text is people: their thoughts, their reasoning, their emotions, the situations they were in, the world they were describing. So prediction, done well enough, forces a kind of compression of all of that into the model. It's a projection of the world onto text, and the model is learning to invert that projection, at least partially.

One of the remarkable things about pre-training is that you don't have to decide what data to use in a careful, curated sense. The answer is just "everything." You don't need to think hard about which skills you want. That's very different from later stages like reinforcement learning, where you have to choose the environments, the tasks, what you're rewarding. Pre-training gives you breadth almost for free.

But I'd add a caveat: it's quite hard to reason about *how* the model is using its pre-training knowledge. When the model makes a mistake, is it because something wasn't in the data, or because it's in the data but the model doesn't generalize from it the way a person would? I think that's an open question. Humans see far, far less data than these models, yet in many ways we understand things more deeply and more robustly. So pre-training is extraordinarily powerful, but it's not obviously the same thing as what humans do, and I think understanding that gap, the difference in generalization, is one of the most important questions right now.

r001.rationale: It says text reflects people’s thoughts, reasoning, emotions, and world, and that the model learns to invert that projection.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says it is hard to reason about how the model uses its pre-training knowledge.

r003.rationale: It raises whether a fact was absent from the data or present but not generalized from; it does not say the fact may be poorly supported there by chance.

r004.rationale: It says pre-training is not obviously the same as what humans do, but does not express that pre-training has no human analog.

fable-5.1.text:
Pre-training, to me, is the thing that gives the model a kind of very broad, dense familiarity with the world as it's reflected in text. The thing that was surprising, and maybe still is surprising, is how much you get just from predicting the next token at scale. People hear "next token prediction" and think it sounds shallow, like a parlor trick. But if you think about what it actually takes to predict the next word well across all of human writing, you realize that to do it well, you have to understand a lot. You have to understand the subject matter, the reasoning that went into the text, the people who wrote it, their intentions, the structure of arguments. The data is a kind of projection of the world, and the model has to build an internal representation of the thing that produced that projection.

So I think of pre-training as compression of the world's text into a model, and good compression requires understanding. That's where the capabilities come from. The model isn't memorizing, it's learning the regularities, and the deeper regularities are things like physics, psychology, mathematics, the way people think.

But pre-training also has a particular character that's worth being honest about. The model learns what the data contains, in the proportions the data contains it. It's not learning because it wants to figure something out. It's learning because that's what the objective is. And so there's a sense in which pre-training gives you an enormous amount of raw ability and knowledge, but not necessarily the thing that makes it useful, or directed, or careful. That's what the later stages are for. Pre-training is the foundation, and I think the quality of that foundation determines what everything on top of it is going to be capable of. If the understanding isn't there in the base model, you can't really add it later with a small amount of fine-tuning.

The other thing I'd say is that we've been riding a very simple idea for a while now, which is that if you make the model bigger and give it more data, it gets better in a fairly predictable way. And that's been true, and it's remarkable that it's been true. But I also think we're going to find that the data is finite in a way that compute is not, and that's going to change how people think about what pre-training is and what it should be. We'll have to get more out of each example, rather than just getting more examples.

r001.rationale: It describes pre-training as giving the model broad familiarity with the world as reflected in text.

r002.rationale: It calls the capabilities from next-token prediction surprising, but does not say it is difficult to understand how a model relies on its pre-training data.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest that a model mistake could result from something being poorly supported by chance in its pre-training data.

r004.rationale: It does not express that pre-training has no human analog.

astra-6.text:
I think of pre-training as a way of turning prediction into learning. You take a neural network and ask it to predict the next token across a very large amount of text. That sounds like a narrow task, but to do it really well, the network has to discover a lot about the processes that produced the text.

For example, if you’re reading a detective story, predicting what happens next may require keeping track of what each character knows, what they want, and what they’re trying to hide. You’re still predicting the next token, but the computation that helps you make that prediction can be much richer.

So pre-training gives the model knowledge, but also ways of representing things and using that knowledge. The important question is how far that goes: when does learning to predict produce an understanding that carries over to a new situation? Memorization can help with familiar examples. But to predict well in unfamiliar situations, you need to learn something more general.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training can teach knowledge and richer ways of representing text, but does not characterize it as capturing the world as represented by people in text.

r002.rationale: It questions how far prediction-based learning generalizes, but does not say it is difficult to understand how a model relies on its pre-training data.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect model mistakes to something being poorly supported by chance in the pre-training data.

r004.rationale: The response makes no claim that pre-training lacks a human analog.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to think about pre-training is that you’re compressing a very large amount of information into the parameters of a neural network. But to compress well, you need to discover the structure in the data. You need to understand something about the processes that produced it.

So, although the objective is to predict the next token, the things you learn can go far beyond superficial patterns in text. If you’re reading a detective story and you want to predict what happens next, it helps to have some understanding of the characters, what they know, and what they’re trying to do. The prediction problem creates an incentive to learn those things.

The interesting question is how far that incentive takes you. How much understanding can you get from trying to predict very accurately? I think the answer is quite a lot, though that doesn’t mean that pre-training alone gives you every capability you might want.

r001.rationale: The response describes compressing information from data and learning about the processes that produced it, but does not clearly characterize pre-training as capturing the world as represented by people in text.

r002.rationale: It asks how far prediction takes a model, but does not say that it is difficult to understand how the model relies on its pre-training data.

r003.rationale: It does not raise the possibility that a model’s mistake reflects something being poorly supported by chance in its pre-training data.

r004.rationale: It does not express the view that pre-training has no human analog.
